clue.text: Direction-finders for a jumping cow?

parts.note: the nursery-rhyme cow jumped over the moon, and radio beams were used to guide aircraft, so the clue imagines lunar guidance beams for her leap

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about navigation aids for a leaping cow.
explanation.walkthrough: In 'Hey Diddle Diddle' the cow jumped over the moon; a beam was a radio signal that steered aircraft, so the cow is steered by the moon's beams.
explanation.definitionFit: Rays of light shining from the earth's satellite, here pictured as radio guidance signals.

clue.text: Orangemen?

parts.note: read as orange men: small citrus fruits that share their name with Chinese officials

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both small loose-skinned citrus fruits and high officials of imperial China.

clue.text: Waiting for the pay off

parts.note: a debt still unpaid is waiting to be settled

explanation.surface: Someone is waiting for a payoff, or to be paid off.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum still due has not yet been settled, so it waits for payment.

clue.text: "He sinks into thy depths with — groan" (Byron)

definitions.text: "He sinks into thy depths with — groan" (Byron)

parts.words: "He sinks into thy depths with — groan" (Byron)
parts.note: a line from the ocean stanzas of Childe Harold, where a drowning man's last breath rises as froth

explanation.surface: A quotation from Byron with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Byron's address to the ocean in Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, canto IV.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adjective describes the frothing, gurgling sound of a drowning man's last breath.

clue.text: The cow that tossed Lady Rene?

indicators.note: tossed means thrown about, so the letters of the woman's name are jumbled

explanation.surface: A cow gores and throws an aristocratic lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossed' is what a cow does with its horns, and also the anagram signal for LADYRENE.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed of dairy cattle from the Channel Island of the same name.

clue.text: Tie up a poor dog, look out!

indicators.note: look out read as the word for look placed on the outside of the next piece

parts.note: look means see
a cur is a worthless mongrel

explanation.surface: A warning shout while tethering a sorry-looking mutt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look out!' reads as a shouted warning, but 'out' is the container signal: the word for 'look' goes outside the poor dog.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten or make fast, as a rope tied to a post.

clue.text: No ploughgirl, according to Browning

parts.note: Browning's verse drama is called ... Passes, and in old university slang to plough is to fail an exam, so a girl who passes is no failure

explanation.surface: A literary remark that some girl in Browning was not a farm worker.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'ploughed' was old British university slang for failing an exam; Browning's heroine, in the title Pippa Passes, does the opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: The silk-mill girl who is the heroine of Robert Browning's dramatic poem Pippa Passes.

clue.text: This hat could carry the Republican ticket

definitions.text: This hat could carry the Republican ticket

parts.words: This hat could carry the Republican ticket
parts.note: the straw hat shares its name with a Central American republic, which could put its label on it

explanation.surface: A hat with a party election label tucked in its band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Republican ticket' looks like US party politics; it is the label of a republic, the country the hat is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: A light woven straw hat, named after the Central American republic.

clue.text: Putting on a show

parts.note: staging a play, or simply bringing something out to be seen

explanation.surface: Someone is showing off.
explanation.definitionFit: Staging a play or film is the work of the impresario, who mounts and finances it.

clue.text: Part of the shank leading to the foot

indicators.note: Part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An anatomy note on the leg running down to the foot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is literally true: the joint links the shank to the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint joining leg and foot, which leads down to the foot.

clue.text: Handy resting-place for an ascetic?

parts.note: a fakir lies on a bed of spikes, while 'handy' points to the hand, where the fingernail rests on its bed of flesh

explanation.surface: A question about a convenient place for a holy man to lie down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handy' seems to mean convenient, but it means on the hand: the bed of skin under a fingernail.
explanation.definitionFit: The tissue beneath a fingernail, here also read as the spiked couch of a fakir.

clue.text: Water-lily growing where the ship is able to come in

parts.note: is able means can
a ship docks when it comes in to berth

explanation.surface: A water plant thriving in a harbour where ships berth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'growing where the ship' simply links the definition to the wordplay and sets the harbour scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Candock is an old country name for the yellow water-lily, whose seed heads look like little cans.

clue.text: An infrequent visitor

parts.note: the proverb speaks of visits like those of heavenly messengers, few and far between

explanation.definitionFit: Heavenly messengers are proverbially rare callers, as in 'angels' visits, few and far between'.

clue.text: It sounds as if the last one down the hole is a bat !

indicators.note: this tells us the next words describe how the answer is said, not how it is spelt

parts.words: the last one down the hole
parts.note: the rodent at the back of the queue into the burrow is the rear mouse

explanation.surface: A puzzling claim that the final mouse into a hole turns out to be a bat.
explanation.walkthrough: Rere-mouse is an old word for a bat; it is said just like 'rear mouse', the mouse at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Reremouse is an archaic English name for the flying mammal, from Old English hreremus.

clue.text: Middle-of-the-road typo?

parts.note: a traffic island sits in the middle of the road, so its inhabitant would be a person living on such an island

explanation.surface: A question about a political moderate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle-of-the-road' looks like moderate politics, but it is literal: a traffic island in mid-street.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who lives on an island, pictured here as dwelling on a traffic island.

clue.text: He's a key man? How amusing, love!

definitions.text: He's a key man? How amusing, love!

parts.words: He's a key man? How amusing, love!
parts.note: the proverb says love laughs at the man who makes locks, since no bolt can keep lovers apart

explanation.surface: A sarcastic reply to someone boasting of their importance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'key man' looks like an important person; it is a maker of keys, and the proverb 'Love laughs at locksmiths' supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman who makes and mends locks and cuts keys.

clue.text: Anna used to have twelve of these

definitions.text: Anna used to have twelve of these

parts.words: Anna used to have twelve of these
parts.note: the anna was an old Indian coin worth twelve of the smallest copper coins

explanation.surface: A woman named Anna once owned a dozen of something, perhaps baked dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Anna looks like a woman's name; it is the old Indian coin, divided into twelve pies.
explanation.definitionFit: The pie was the smallest copper coin of British India, a twelfth of an anna.

clue.text: A drink for the talkative Heraclitus

definitions.meaning: an evening glass taken as the sun sets
in Cory's poem the friends 'tired the sun with talking and sent him down the sky'

explanation.walkthrough: William Cory's poem 'Heraclitus' recalls how the two friends talked until they sent the sun down the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: An evening drink at dusk, and literally one who sends the sun down, as Heraclitus did by talking.

clue.text: But you can't leave your car where you like in it

definitions.text: But you can't leave your car where you like in it

parts.words: But you can't leave your car where you like in it
parts.note: the London street's name suggests a place to leave a car, yet stopping there is forbidden

explanation.surface: A grumble about parking restrictions on a busy street.
explanation.walkthrough: PARK LANE is a grand London street beside Hyde Park whose name promises parking it does not allow.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous road in London's Mayfair, running along the east side of Hyde Park.

clue.text: Colourful nonconformist follower of Robert

parts.note: the Elizabethan separatist preacher Robert Browne gave his followers a name that begins with a colour

explanation.surface: A flamboyant dissenter who follows a man called Robert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colourful' seems to mean flamboyant; it says the name starts with a colour, brown.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Robert Browne, founder of an early English Congregationalist sect.

clue.text: A fiery wino?

parts.note: the word is both an old Spanish wine, as drunk by Falstaff, and dismissal, being fired from a job

explanation.surface: A question about a hot-tempered drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack was the old name for sherry, and getting the sack means being fired; the clue fuses the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Sack is the Shakespearean name for dry white wine from Spain, and also dismissal from work.

clue.text: Artemisia's poorly-dressed sailor

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is the plant genus Artemisia

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
with a rag on, wearing tatters

explanation.surface: Someone named Artemisia has a sailor who dresses shabbily.
explanation.walkthrough: Artemisia looks like a woman's name but is the botanical genus of wormwood and its kin; the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The culinary herb belongs to the genus Artemisia, as Artemisia dracunculus.

clue.text: Injure, perhaps, in the devil manner

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
an air is a person's manner or bearing

explanation.surface: Someone does harm in a fiendish way.
explanation.definitionFit: To damage or weaken something is to harm it.

clue.text: "Sir, sit up" the creature seems to pray

parts.note: sir and man are both ways of addressing a fellow

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word sit is written bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A command to sit up, followed by the creature apparently praying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses 'sit' because this is a down clue. 'seems to pray' describes the insect, which holds its forelegs folded as if in prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: A predatory insect whose folded forelegs make it look as though it is praying.

clue.text: Should a mad risk be taken? Come off it!

indicators.note: taken here means taken apart, so the letters of the words before it are pulled about

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a reckless gamble is worth it and is told not to be absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come off it!' reads as a scornful retort, but it means leave the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To go ashore from a vessel is to leave it, to get off.

clue.text: Bird with drumsticks

definitions.meaning: Sir Francis ... drum, said to beat when England is in danger

explanation.definitionFit: A male duck, and the Elizabethan admiral whose famous drum still hangs at Buckland Abbey.

clue.text: He came between Ralph and Emerson

definitions.text: He came between Ralph and Emerson

parts.words: He came between Ralph and Emerson
parts.note: the American essayist's full name puts a middle name between his first name and surname

explanation.surface: A man intervened between two people called Ralph and Emerson.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like someone parting two friends; it is the middle name of Ralph Waldo Emerson, the American essayist.
explanation.definitionFit: The American writer was christened Ralph Waldo Emerson, so this name sits in the middle.

clue.text: In which Madeline slept an azure-lidded sleep

definitions.text: In which Madeline slept an azure-lidded sleep

parts.words: In which Madeline slept an azure-lidded sleep
parts.note: Keats's heroine in The Eve of St Agnes sleeps 'in blanched' sheets of this fabric

explanation.surface: A quotation about Madeline's sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: In Keats's The Eve of St Agnes, 'still she slept an azure-lidded sleep, In blanched linen, smooth, and lavender'd'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth woven from flax, used for bed sheets.

clue.text: A Mohammedan is unable to take this wine

parts.note: Ali is a common Muslim name, after the Prophet's son-in-law
is unable means can't

explanation.surface: A Muslim cannot drink this wine, since alcohol is forbidden.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: Islam forbids alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Alicant is the old English spelling of the red wine from Alicante in Spain.

clue.text: Where to go for bridge and dancing in France

definitions.text: Where to go for bridge and dancing in France

parts.words: Where to go for bridge and dancing in France
parts.note: the French nursery song 'Sur le pont' has people dancing on a famous broken bridge over the Rhone

explanation.surface: Advice on a French town for card games and dances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' looks like the card game; it is the Pont Saint-Benezet of the song 'Sur le pont d'Avignon, on y danse'.
explanation.definitionFit: A city of Provence on the Rhone, famous for its medieval bridge and the song about dancing there.

clue.text: The upper air thereabouts

annotationWithheld.why: The upper air thereabouts (5): the only parse is THERE anagrammed, with 'thereabouts' giving both the fodder THERE and the anagram signal 'abouts', one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Bribe — with sugar?

definitions.meaning: a sum paid to win someone over
something added to make food or drink taste sweet, as sugar does

explanation.definitionFit: A bribe is a gift that makes a deal palatable, and sugar or saccharin makes tea taste nicer.
